title: ANCOVA / MANOVA Decision Laboratory
summary: Assign a role to every variable in a fictional evaluation, then choose an analysis. See what a covariate buys under random allocation, and what it cannot buy with intact groups.
learningObjectives: Assign the roles of outcome, grouping factor and covariate in a described design.
Explain that a covariate's main contribution under randomisation is precision rather than correction.
State what an adjusted difference estimates and when it cannot be read as a causal effect.
State the homogeneity-of-regression-slopes assumption and describe what its failure costs.
Explain why a multivariate test is not several univariate tests bundled together or a multiplicity correction.
interactionTypes: live simulation with a real analysis of generated data
covariate scatterplot with two fitted lines
two-outcome cloud plot with worked examples
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every observation is generated in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, selects, radio groups and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend; every slider announces a meaningful value such as 'the programme group starts -10 points from the other group in September'. Both scatterplots are hidden from assistive technology and paired inside their figures with visible tables - group means and each group's own slope for the covariate plot, and the three separations for the two-outcome plot - and a disclosure reports the gap between the fitted lines at a low, average and high covariate value so a violated slopes assumption can be read as numbers rather than seen as a shape. The two groups are told apart by marker shape, filled circles against hollow triangles, as well as by colour, and both fitted lines are named at their right-hand ends and differ in dash pattern. Signed quantities print an explicit plus or minus. Pinned primary results measure 475px and 417px tall at 1366x768. Every slider, preset, design change and resample announces a full sentence through the polite live region, focus moves to each experiment's heading as it opens, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll. Adjustment opens with three controls - how well the covariate predicts, how far apart the groups already were, and how the groups were formed. The true effect size and the slope difference that breaks the assumption sit behind a disclosure. Controls held back sit inside native <details> elements, reachable by keyboard in one step and announced as collapsed rather than being disabled.
readmeTopic: What a covariate is for, when adjustment misleads, and why MANOVA is not several ANOVAs at once
simulationNotes: Experiment 1 generates two groups of forty. The covariate has mean 50 and standard deviation 10, shifted apart by the group-gap slider; the outcome is 50 plus the group's own slope times the centred covariate, plus half the stated effect in each direction, plus normal noise with standard deviation 10 times the square root of one minus r squared, so that with equal slopes the within-group correlation is r and both variables have standard deviation about 10. Each group's slope is r plus or minus half the slope-difference slider, so the average slope stays at r. The tool then computes, from the generated sample, the unadjusted difference, the pooled within-group slope and the adjusted difference as the unadjusted difference minus that slope times the covariate gap - which is exactly the common-slope ANCOVA adjusted mean difference - together with each group's own slope and the vertical gap between the two fitted lines at three covariate values. The how-groups-were-formed menu changes nothing computational and only what the adjusted number is allowed to mean, which is the honest state of affairs. Experiment 2 draws two standardised outcomes from a bivariate normal with the stated within-group correlation, shifting the group centres by the two standardised differences, and reports the Mahalanobis distance, which equals the square root of (d1 squared minus twice rho d1 d2 plus d2 squared) over one minus rho squared. No F, Wilks lambda or p-value is reported anywhere, because the teaching point is what the quantities mean rather than whether they clear a threshold. Randomness is seeded with mulberry32 and Box-Muller normals. No real study, participant, programme or dataset is involved.
